profile.campus: Prime Dallas, TX campus (DFW01-01, operational/leased, and DFW01-02, under construction, 20 MW / 213,000 sqft combined per Prime own site)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading: Prime DFW01-01 sits at 1515 Round Table Drive in Dallas, Texas, part of a two-building Prime Data Centers campus in that market. Per Prime own Dallas locations page, DFW01-01 provides 8 megawatts of capacity across 107,000 square feet and is operational and leased, while a second building on the same campus, DFW01-02 at 1455 Round Table Drive, adds a further 12 megawatts across 96,000 square feet and remains under construction, bringing the full campus to a planned 20 megawatts and 213,000 square feet. A January 2026 Prime press release confirms DFW01-01 operational status by name, reporting that the facility earned ENERGY STAR certification for superior energy performance alongside a Prime facility in Sacramento, though that release does not disclose additional capacity or tenant detail. This exact OpenStreetMap record shares its name, reference designation, and Round Table Drive address with a second nearby way in this same dataset, mapped roughly 100 to 150 meters away in a December 2025 changeset by the same contributor, and since Prime own site describes DFW01-01 as a single 107,000 square foot building rather than two, that companion record most plausibly reflects a mapping artifact, such as a duplicated or split campus footprint, rather than two genuinely separate leasable buildings, though this could not be confirmed with certainty this session. No tenant is named for DFW01-01. Prime Data Centers was founded in 2017 in California and is now headquartered at 400 North Ervay Street in Dallas, Texas, describing itself as majority founder-owned and led by founder and CEO Nicholas Laag, with an overall footprint of 28 data centers across 13 campuses and a pipeline exceeding 4 gigawatts spanning Austin, Chicago, Dallas, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Sacramento, Silicon Valley, Frankfurt, Madrid, and a newly announced site in Esbjerg, Denmark.
profile.campus_note: One of 2 buildings OpenStreetMap contributors have mapped under this name in this locality, numbered west to east.
profile.research_note: 8 MW / 107,000 sqft / operational-leased status sourced to Prime own Dallas locations page, corroborated by a Jan 2026 ENERGY STAR press release naming DFW01-01 specifically. A companion OSM record with the identical name/address exists nearby, most plausibly a mapping artifact since Prime describes only one 107,000 sqft DFW01-01 building, flagged honestly as unresolved with certainty rather than asserted either way.

reading.body:
Prime DFW01-01 publishes 20 MW of IT capacity across 213,000 square feet of technical space in Dallas, with a power density that suggests mixed or general-purpose colocation rather than dense AI training clusters.

At 40 kW per rack, the published 20 MW supports roughly 500 racks; at 10 kW per rack, it supports roughly 2,000 racks. The operator has not published a target rack density, so which assumption applies remains unknown. The 94 watts per square foot working out from the published IT load ranks toward the lower end of AI-optimized facilities, implying the space may be sized for enterprise workloads across multiple use cases rather than concentrated GPU deployments. This inference depends on layout assumptions the operator has not disclosed.

SOC 2 Type 2 certification indicates the facility passed independent audit of security controls over a defined period, qualifying it for regulated enterprise workloads. ISO 27001 certification shows implementation of an audited information security management system. Neither certification speaks to power redundancy tier or cooling capacity, the infrastructure that determines whether this site can sustain the continuous demand AI training requires.

Within Texas, this facility ranks sixth among thirteen sites that have published a megawatt figure out of 133 total mapped facilities in the state. The thirteen published facilities account for 389 MW in aggregate; DFW01-01's 20 MW represents roughly 5 percent of that disclosed total. The remaining 120 mapped Texas facilities have published no capacity, so the 389 MW understates true state capacity by an unknown margin, and the sixth-place rank reflects only what operators chose to disclose rather than actual scale.
